lead: Named entity recognition (NER) finds the runs of words in a text that name a person, a place, an organisation, a date, an amount and similar things, and labels each run with its category. It exists because most later work — search, question answering, news indexing, form filling — needs the actors in a sentence, not only its grammar. A bank's KYC team, a newsroom sorting stories by company, and a chatbot reading 'pay ₹500 to Ravi on Friday' all sit on top of NER. It is usually solved as sequence labelling: one tag per token.
prereq: You need: 2.4 for the idea of a tagset, and 2.7 (with 2.5) for the sequence models that do the labelling.

blocks.text: A named entity is a contiguous run of tokens that names one specific thing. NER does two jobs at once: it finds where each run starts and ends, and it puts the run into a category. Both jobs are hard. 'Apple' is a fruit in one sentence and a company in the next.

Four types cover most news and office text. PERSON (PER) names a person, for example 'Sundar Pichai'. LOCATION (LOC) names a place, natural or political, for example 'Godavari' or 'Pune'. ORGANISATION (ORG) names a company, team, agency or institution, for example 'IRCTC' or 'State Bank of India'. MISCELLANEOUS (MISC) is the leftover bin for named things that are none of these — events, laws, awards, nationalities, such as 'Kumbh Mela' or 'Bharat Ratna'.

A second family holds numeric and temporal expressions, where the value matters more than the name: DATE ('12 March 2024'), TIME ('4:30 pm'), MONEY ('₹2,500'), PERCENT ('18%'). A form-filling system wants these with a normalised value, so the tagger often writes 12/03/2024 next to the span.

The tagset is a design choice, not a law. Standard shared-task tagsets use PER, LOC, ORG and MISC; a bank may add ACCOUNT and IFSC_CODE. Changing the tagset changes the scores, so always report which one you used.

A sequence labeller gives one tag per token, so the tag itself must carry both the type and the boundary. BIO does this with a prefix. B-X means 'this token begins an entity of type X'. I-X means 'this token continues an entity of type X'. O means 'outside every entity'.

The B prefix is not decoration. Two entities of the same type can sit side by side: In 'Delhi Mumbai flights', Delhi and Mumbai are two places with no word between them. With only I-LOC the two names merge into one span. B-LOC restarts the span, so the boundary survives.

Some taggers use BIOES, also written BILOU. E-X ends an entity and S-X is a single-token entity. The end markers state the right boundary outright, so the model need not infer it from the next token being O. Sequences must obey the scheme: I-X may not follow O or B-Y when Y is not X. A CRF can be given a very large penalty for those transitions, so its decoder can never emit an illegal sequence.
The boundary problem appears whenever entities touch or one is a piece of another, as in 'Wipro Limited Chennai'. Exact-span scoring then punishes a run that is split differently from the gold data.

sections.h3: Three ways to build a tagger

blocks.text: Gazetteer and rules. Keep lists of known persons, cities and companies. Add patterns: a capitalised word after 'Mr' is PER; a listed city after 'in' is LOC; a capitalised word ending in 'Ltd' or 'Pvt' is ORG. This is fast and precise on known names, and it never generalises to a name that was added yesterday.

Features plus a classifier. Turn each token into a feature vector and predict its tag. Useful features: the word itself; its lowercase form; word shape (Xxx for 'Pune', XX for 'TCS', dd for a number); capitalisation flags; a prefix and suffix of three or four letters (-pur, -abad, -son, Ltd); the previous and next word; membership of a gazetteer; and the previous tag. The previous tag is what makes this sequence labelling — the classifier sees the decisions already made.

The CRF of 2.7 is the standard non-neural model here: it accepts overlapping features and scores the whole tag sequence, so neighbour tags enter each decision properly. A maximum entropy Markov model (2.6) also works and is cheaper to train. A plain HMM (2.5) sees only the current word through its emission table, so it cannot use the suffix of the next word or the previous two tags.
Token accuracy is the wrong metric. A tagger that prints O everywhere scores about 90% on newswire, because most tokens lie outside entities, and it finds nothing at all.

Score whole entities with exact-span matching: a predicted entity is correct only if its start, end and type all match a gold entity. Let C be the number of such matches, N the number of predicted entities and G the number of gold entities.
P = C ÷ N,  R = C ÷ G,  F1 = 2PR ÷ (P + R)
blocks.where: P is precision, R is recall, C is the count of exactly matching entities, N is the number of entities the system predicted, G is the number of entities in the gold annotation; F1 is their harmonic mean, all three between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: One wrong boundary word costs twice: the gold entity is missed, which lowers recall, and a wrong span is invented, which lowers precision.

examples.question: Tag the sentence 'Mr Rao of TCS met the team in Pune' with BIO labels over the types PER, ORG and LOC. A system then predicts the entities Rao (PER), TCS (ORG) and the span 'team in Pune' (LOC). The gold entities are Rao (PER), TCS (ORG) and Pune (LOC); 'the team' is not an entity. Compute precision, recall and F1 under exact-span matching.
steps: Tokenise: Mr, Rao, of, TCS, met, the, team, in, Pune — 9 tokens.

Tag each token. The title 'Mr' is outside the span, so it is O. 'Rao' begins a person. 'TCS' begins an organisation. 'Pune' is a one-token location, which gets B-LOC (BIOES would write S-LOC). Full line: Mr/O Rao/B-PER of/O TCS/B-ORG met/O the/O team/O in/O Pune/B-LOC.
Read off the gold spans: gold G = {(Rao, PER), (TCS, ORG), (Pune, LOC)}, so G = 3 entities.
Read off the system spans: predicted N = {(Rao, PER), (TCS, ORG), (team in Pune, LOC)}, so N = 3 entities.
Match exactly: (Rao, PER) and (TCS, ORG) match, giving C = 2. 'team in Pune' has the right type but the wrong boundary, so it is a false positive, and Pune is a false negative.
examples.answer: Precision = 0.67, recall = 0.67 and F1 = 0.67; the wrong boundary on 'team in Pune' produces one false positive and one false negative at the same time.
examples.check:
gold = [('Rao','PER'), ('TCS','ORG'), ('Pune','LOC')]
pred = [('Rao','PER'), ('TCS','ORG'), ('team in Pune','LOC')]
C = len(set(gold) & set(pred))
N = len(pred)
G = len(gold)
P = C / N
R = C / G
F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R)
print(f"{P:.2f}")
print(f"{R:.2f}")
print(f"{F1:.2f}")

traps: Grading token by token: an all-O tagger gets about 90% token accuracy and F1 = 0. Reporting accuracy alone for NER is the classic mistake.
One boundary word wrong destroys a whole entity under exact-span matching, and it counts twice — one false positive and one false negative.
Writing I-PER on the first token of an entity is an illegal sequence; gold data never has I-X straight after O.
Partial overlap is not a match: 'Bank of India' against gold 'Reserve Bank of India' scores zero for that entity, not half.
Capitalisation features fail outside English and outside edited text — Hindi or Tamil has no case, and chat text is lowercase throughout.

quiz.q: Define named entity recognition in one sentence.
quiz.a: It finds spans of text that name entities and assigns each span a type such as person, location or organisation.

quiz.q: What do B, I and O stand for in BIO tagging?
quiz.a: B is begin, I is inside (continue), O is outside every entity.

quiz.q: Why is B needed when I already carries the entity type?
quiz.a: Two entities of the same type can touch, as in 'Delhi Mumbai flights'. With only I-LOC the two names merge into one span; B-LOC restarts it.

quiz.q: Tag 'Ms Iyer flew from Delhi to Wipro office in Bengaluru' with BIO labels over PER, LOC and ORG.
quiz.a: Ms/O Iyer/B-PER flew/O from/O Delhi/B-LOC to/O Wipro/B-ORG office/O in/O Bengaluru/B-LOC. As with 'Mr' in the worked example, the title 'Ms' stays outside the person span, so it is O.

quiz.q: Gold holds 5 entities. A system predicts 6 entities, of which 4 match gold exactly. Give P, R and F1.
A system tags every token O and reports 91% token accuracy. What is its entity F1, and what does the number show?
quiz.a: It predicts no entities, so correct matches C = 0, precision is 0 (no predictions), recall is 0, F1 = 0. The 91% only says most tokens are outside entities; the metric measures tags, not entities, so it cannot see the failure.

quiz.q: Why does the previous tag help a feature-based NER classifier more than the next word alone?
quiz.a: The previous tag records whether an entity is already open, so the model can keep a name going or close it. The next word gives one-sided evidence only; it cannot say whether a span has started.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, NER is now mostly a token-classification head on a pretrained transformer: fine-tune a BERT-style encoder on a few thousand annotated sentences and it beats feature-based CRFs on most domains. Indic-language NER remains an open problem, because there is no capitalisation cue, names transliterate several ways, and annotated data is thin outside news. Data-hungry teams generate weak labels from gazetteers and then clean them, or transfer a multilingual model. Downstream, the extracted entities feed relation extraction and entity linking, which attaches each mention to a knowledge-base identifier. Search terms: CoNLL-2003, BIO tagging, token classification, multilingual NER, distant supervision.
